analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity in workplaces, housing, stores, credit, and jury service.
analysis.headline: Every one of the bill's 218 cosponsors is a Democrat, and since its April 2025 introduction it has sat in five House committees without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act would write sexual orientation and gender identity protections into the nation's core civil rights laws, alongside race, religion, and national origin. It would bar discrimination in employment, housing, credit, jury selection, federally funded programs, and public accommodations — a category it expands to cover nearly any business serving the public, including stores, banks, shelters, transportation, and health care providers. It defines sex to include pregnancy, sex stereotypes, and sex characteristics, and it says federal religious-freedom law cannot be used as a defense against these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people and women who face discrimination at work, when renting or buying housing, when seeking credit, when being served by stores, shelters, and health providers, or when serving on juries. The bill's findings cite studies showing transgender people have roughly half the homeownership rate of non-transgender people and that same-sex couples frequently receive worse responses from landlords. Federal workers and congressional employees get the same explicit protections as private-sector workers.

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to Titles II, IV, VI, and VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and to the Fair Housing Act, so discrimination in schools, housing, employment, and federally funded programs is explicitly illegal nationwide.

Expands 'public accommodations' to cover stores, online retailers, banks, salons, shelters, transportation, funeral parlors, and providers of health care, accounting, or legal services — and makes clear the ban applies to individuals providing goods and services, not just physical buildings.
Prohibits discrimination by creditors and bars lawyers from removing jurors because of actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity.

Defines sex to include sex stereotypes, pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions, sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, and requires that pregnancy receive no less favorable treatment than other medical conditions.
Requires that individuals be allowed access to shared restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms consistent with their gender identity.
Blocks the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a claim or defense against the law's prohibitions.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that serve the public — retailers, landlords, lenders, employers, shelters, and health care and professional service providers — would face new obligations and potential lawsuits. Religious institutions and faith-based child welfare agencies that object to serving same-sex couples or transgender people would lose their ability to raise a Religious Freedom Restoration Act defense. Small businesses would bear compliance and litigation costs, and organizations that currently restrict foster or adoptive placements would have to change their practices.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 of any role as a claim or defense under the covered titles, which religious schools, faith-based adoption and foster agencies, and religious objectors argue removes their legal protection to act on their beliefs in hiring, placement, and service decisions.

The definition of an 'establishment' includes any individual providing a good, service, or program, and covers online retailers and service providers, which critics say sweeps nearly every exchange in the economy into public accommodations law and expands litigation exposure far beyond the storefronts covered by the 1964 Act.

The rule granting facility access consistent with gender identity — restrooms, locker rooms, dressing rooms — is the provision opponents most frequently contest, particularly as applied to schools and women's facilities.
Businesses, especially small ones, would bear new compliance costs and discrimination-claim exposure across employment, housing, credit, and service provisions simultaneously.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real and address discrimination that the bill's own findings document with federal housing studies and poverty data. The costs fall on businesses through compliance and litigation and, most sharply, on religious objectors through the elimination of the RFRA defense — a deliberate trade-off supporters accept rather than an oversight. The facility-access provision is genuinely contested and has driven most of the political opposition. On balance, the bill delivers substantial legal protection to a group with documented, measurable disadvantages, at a concentrated cost to service providers and religious institutions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to five House committees in April 2025, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in a House controlled by Republicans, none of whom support it.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Equality Act on April 29, 2025, and it was referred to the Judiciary, Education and Workforce, Financial Services, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform committees, with scheduling left to the Speaker's designation.
The bill drew 218 cosponsors, all from the Democratic side — the full non-Republican membership of the chamber — and no Republican cosponsor.
No further action appears in the bill's history after the April 29 referrals: no committee has taken it up and no vote has occurred.

The bill would amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Fair Housing Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and federal jury-selection law to prohibit discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, the status quo holds: businesses, landlords, lenders, and religious objectors remain under current law, while LGBTQ people retain existing protections (including the Supreme Court's Bostock ruling on employment) without the new statutory guarantees.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Service providers and religious objectors, under the status quo

for.name: 218 House Democrats and independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every one of the 218 cosponsors is from the Democratic side, including the party leadership.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 218 cosponsors, none Republican — and the Republican majority of 223 has taken no action on the bill since it was referred to committee.

industries.note: Stores, online retailers, banks, shelters, transportation providers, and health, accounting, and legal service firms would all be subject to public accommodations and employment nondiscrimination law, with litigation exposure. Their interest in operating free of these obligations runs against customers' and workers' equal treatment.

industries.industry: Religious schools and faith-based child welfare agencies
industries.note: The bill removes the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense, so agencies that restrict foster or adoptive placements, hiring, or services on religious grounds could no longer raise that claim; the bill's findings argue barring such discrimination would increase the pool of homes for children in foster care.
Landlords and creditors could not consider sexual orientation or gender identity, or a person's association with someone, in renting, selling, or extending credit.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 223 House seats, no Republican cosponsor, and the bill parked across five committees with no scheduled action, it is very unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote in this Congress. A prior version passed the House when Democrats held the majority in 2019 but never became law; the realistic best case here is reintroduction if chamber control changes.
